implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines supplies both halves of the processor: `Channel<Command>` is the repository (capacity-bounded, `send` suspends when full, which is exactly the backpressure policy) and a coroutine launched in a `SupervisorJob` scope draining `for (cmd in channel)` is the executor; `sealed interface Command` plus an exhaustive `when` replaces the Command subclasses, and `suspend` handlers let a command block on I/O without occupying a thread. Structured concurrency also replaces the classic start/stop protocol - cancelling the processor scope cancels its workers and their children. Undo is still application logic: keep a stack of inverse suspend functions alongside the channel, since coroutines carry no history. Explicit Command objects with an execute() method are still justified when commands must be persisted, versioned or selected by name from configuration (kotlinx.serialization plus a registry), because a sealed interface alone carries no wire format.
pitfalls: GlobalScope.launch leaks the worker past the component's lifetime; use a scoped CoroutineScope and cancel it (or Channel.close()) on shutdown.
`trySend` on a full channel returns a failure result that is easy to ignore, silently dropping commands; `Channel.UNLIMITED` removes backpressure altogether.
An `else ->` branch in the `when` defeats the exhaustiveness check that makes newly added commands fail fast at compile time.
A command that blocks a Dispatchers.Default thread (JDBC, file I/O) starves the CPU pool; switch to Dispatchers.IO or make the handler genuinely suspend.
